summary:
The Secure America Act provides for direct appropriations to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for fiscal year 2026, enacted as reconciliation legislation pursuant to S. Con. Res. 33. The Act’s operative mechanism is supplemental, multi-year appropriations—available until September 30, 2029—drawn from the general fund, with purpose-specific use restrictions.

Title I (Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs):
Section 101 appropriates $9,550,000,000 to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel for functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions, with a restriction that after October 31, 2028, none of the funds may be used to recruit, hire, or train processing coordinators.
Section 102 appropriates $7,450,000,000 to the Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents, support personnel, and necessary expenses for HSI mission support and operations and maintenance, explicitly excluding immigration and customs enforcement missions. Of this amount, $108,500,000 is directed to hiring and equipping additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts at specified HSI units and for related training, including for state and local law enforcement.
Section 103 appropriates $3,450,000,000 to the CBP Commissioner for enumerated purposes: procurement and integration of nonintrusive inspection equipment with AI and machine learning; upgrading air and marine platforms; border surveillance technology procurement; expenses for the biometric entry-exit system under 8 U.S.C. 1365b; combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and precursors; and mission support and operations and maintenance for non-immigration and non-customs functions. It restricts procurement or deployment of autonomous surveillance towers not meeting CBP testing and acceptance standards and defines “autonomous” as a system applying specified algorithms that can make operational adjustments without active personnel engagement or continuous human control.
Section 104 appropriates $2,500,000,000 to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the purposes of Title I.

Title II (Committee on the Judiciary):
Section 201 appropriates $13,020,000,000 to the CBP Commissioner for hiring, paying, training, and equipping CBP agents and support staff and for mission support and operations and maintenance to carry out immigration enforcement activities.
Section 202 appropriates $31,075,000,000 to the ICE Director for nine specified immigration enforcement purposes: personnel hiring and equipping across all directorates; transportation for removals; information technology; facility and fleet maintenance; expanding section 287(g) agreements (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)); hiring attorneys for the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor; mission support and operations and maintenance; and, within this amount, not less than $350,000,000 for operations to arrest covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions, subject to a limitation prohibiting the use of such funds to release or facilitate release of any covered unlawful alien. The term “qualified cooperating jurisdiction” is defined as a State or political subdivision that either has an active 287(g) agreement or has certified compliance with 8 U.S.C. 1373 and 8 U.S.C. 1644; Indian tribal governments are excluded from treatment as non-qualified. “Covered unlawful alien” is defined by cross-reference to criminal and security-related inadmissibility and deportability grounds, certain immigration detainers following criminal arrests, and aliens charged with or convicted of offenses under 8 U.S.C. 1325 or 1326.
Section 203 appropriates $2,500,000,000 to the Secretary of Homeland Security for the purposes of Title II or specific paragraphs in Public Law 119-21.
